title: Light – Reflection and Refraction
description: Class 10 Physics Light: laws of reflection, spherical mirrors, mirror formula, magnification, refraction, Snell's law and lenses with ray diagrams, solved numericals and tests.

topics.title: Reflection & Spherical Mirrors
topics.concept:
When light falls on a polished surface it bounces back into the same medium — this turning back of light is called reflection. The ray that strikes the surface is the incident ray, the one that bounces off is the reflected ray, and the line drawn perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence is the normal. Two laws govern every reflection, whether from a plane mirror or a curved one.

The laws of reflection are:

  • The angle of incidence ($\angle i$) is always equal to the angle of reflection ($\angle r$), i.e. $\angle i = \angle r$.
  • The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.

A plane mirror gives an image that is virtual, erect, the same size as the object and laterally inverted, formed as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. Curved mirrors are far more useful. A spherical mirror is a small part of a hollow sphere whose one surface is silvered. If the reflecting surface is the inner (caved-in) side it is a concave mirror; if it is the bulged-out side it is a convex mirror.

Key terms for a spherical mirror are worth memorising. The pole (P) is the centre of the mirror's reflecting surface. The centre of curvature (C) is the centre of the sphere of which the mirror is a part, and the radius of curvature (R) is the distance PC. The principal axis is the straight line passing through P and C. The principal focus (F) is the point on the principal axis where rays parallel to the axis meet (concave) or appear to diverge from (convex) after reflection. The distance PF is the focal length (f), and for a spherical mirror $f = \frac{R}{2}$.

Two simple ray rules let you draw any image. A ray parallel to the principal axis passes through F (or appears to come from F) after reflection; a ray through C (or directed towards C) returns along the same path because it strikes the mirror normally. In a concave mirror, the nature, position and size of the image change as the object moves from infinity towards the pole — it can be real and inverted, or virtual and enlarged when the object is between P and F. A convex mirror always gives a virtual, erect, diminished image, which is why it is used as a rear-view mirror and at blind corners. Concave mirrors are used in torches, shaving mirrors, headlights and solar furnaces.

examples.problem: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror at an angle of incidence of $35^\circ$. What is the angle of reflection, and what is the angle between the incident and reflected rays?
examples.solution:
1. By the first law of reflection, $\angle r = \angle i = 35^\circ$.
  2. The angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray $= \angle i + \angle r = 35^\circ + 35^\circ$.
  3. $= 70^\circ$.

Answer: Angle of reflection $= 35^\circ$; angle between the rays $= 70^\circ$.

examples.problem: The radius of curvature of a concave mirror is $30\,\text{cm}$. Find its focal length.
examples.solution:
1. For a spherical mirror, $f = \frac{R}{2}$.
  2. $f = \frac{30}{2} = 15\,\text{cm}$.

Answer: Focal length $= 15\,\text{cm}$.

examples.problem: A spherical mirror has a focal length of $20\,\text{cm}$. What is its radius of curvature?
examples.solution:
1. Since $f = \frac{R}{2}$, we have $R = 2f$.
  2. $R = 2 \times 20 = 40\,\text{cm}$.

Answer: Radius of curvature $= 40\,\text{cm}$.

examples.problem: An object is placed beyond the centre of curvature of a concave mirror. Describe the nature, position and size of the image.
examples.solution:
1. When the object is beyond C, the two standard rays (parallel ray through F, and ray through C) meet between F and C.
  2. The image is therefore formed between F and C.
  3. It is real (rays actually meet), inverted, and diminished (smaller than the object).

Answer: Real, inverted and diminished, formed between F and C.

examples.problem: Why is a convex mirror preferred as a rear-view mirror in vehicles?
examples.solution:
1. A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image, whatever the position of the object.
  2. Because the image is diminished, the mirror covers a much wider field of view than a plane mirror of the same size.
  3. The driver can therefore see a larger area of traffic behind the vehicle in a small mirror.

Answer: It gives an erect, diminished image and a wide field of view, so more traffic is visible behind the vehicle.

examples.problem: An object is placed between the pole and the focus of a concave mirror. State the nature and size of the image formed.
examples.solution:
1. When the object lies between P and F, the reflected rays diverge and do not meet in front of the mirror.
  2. On extending them backwards they appear to meet behind the mirror.
  3. So the image is virtual and erect, and it is larger than the object (magnified).

Answer: Virtual, erect and magnified, formed behind the mirror.

recap: Laws of reflection: angle of incidence equals angle of reflection ($\angle i = \angle r$), and incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane.
A concave mirror reflects from the caved-in surface; a convex mirror reflects from the bulged-out surface.
Key terms: pole (P), centre of curvature (C), radius of curvature (R), principal axis, principal focus (F) and focal length (f).
A convex mirror always gives a virtual, erect, diminished image; a concave mirror's image depends on object position.

quiz.q: The laws of reflection hold for:
quiz.explanation: The laws of reflection apply to every reflecting surface, plane or curved.

quiz.q: The relation between focal length and radius of curvature of a spherical mirror is:
quiz.explanation: For a spherical mirror the focal length is half the radius of curvature, $f = \frac{R}{2}$.

quiz.q: Which mirror always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image?
quiz.explanation: A convex mirror gives a virtual, erect, diminished image for every object position.

quiz.q: An object placed between the pole and focus of a concave mirror forms an image that is:
quiz.explanation: When the object is between P and F, a concave mirror forms a virtual, erect and magnified image behind the mirror.

topics.title: Mirror Formula & Magnification
topics.concept:
Drawing ray diagrams tells us the nature of an image, but to find exact distances we need numbers and a consistent sign system. The New Cartesian Sign Convention fixes the rules. The pole of the mirror is taken as the origin and the principal axis as the x-axis. All distances are measured from the pole. Distances measured against the direction of incident light (i.e. to the left, behind the mirror in the usual diagram) are negative, while distances measured along the incident light are positive. Heights measured upwards (above the axis) are positive and those measured downwards are negative.

Because the object is always placed in front of a mirror, the object distance $u$ is always negative. A concave mirror has a negative focal length; a convex mirror has a positive focal length. These signs are not optional — putting in the wrong sign is the single most common mistake in numericals.

The mirror formula links the object distance, image distance and focal length:

  • $\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$, where $v$ is the image distance, $u$ is the object distance and $f$ is the focal length.

The magnification (m) tells us how large the image is compared with the object, and whether it is erect or inverted. It is defined as the ratio of image height $h'$ to object height $h$, and is also related to the distances:

  • $m = \frac{h'}{h} = -\frac{v}{u}$.

The sign of $m$ carries meaning. A negative magnification means the image is real and inverted; a positive magnification means the image is virtual and erect. If $|m| > 1$ the image is enlarged, if $|m| < 1$ it is diminished, and if $|m| = 1$ it is the same size as the object. To solve a numerical, first write down every known quantity with its correct sign, substitute into the mirror formula to find the unknown distance, and then use the magnification relation. Always interpret the final signs to describe the image fully — never report a bare number without saying whether the image is real or virtual, erect or inverted.

examples.problem: An object is placed $20\,\text{cm}$ in front of a concave mirror of focal length $15\,\text{cm}$. Find the position of the image.
examples.solution:
1. Sign convention: $u = -20\,\text{cm}$, $f = -15\,\text{cm}$ (concave).
  2. Mirror formula: $\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$, so $\frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{f} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{-15} - \frac{1}{-20}$.
  3. $\frac{1}{v} = -\frac{1}{15} + \frac{1}{20} = \frac{-4 + 3}{60} = -\frac{1}{60}$.
  4. $v = -60\,\text{cm}$.

Answer: $v = -60\,\text{cm}$ — the image is real, formed $60\,\text{cm}$ in front of the mirror.

examples.problem: For the mirror in Example 1 ($u = -20\,\text{cm}$, $v = -60\,\text{cm}$), find the magnification and describe the image.
examples.solution:
1. Magnification $m = -\frac{v}{u} = -\frac{-60}{-20}$.
  2. $m = -\frac{60}{20} = -3$.
  3. The magnification is negative, so the image is real and inverted; $|m| = 3 > 1$, so it is enlarged three times.

Answer: $m = -3$; the image is real, inverted and three times the size of the object.

examples.problem: An object $5\,\text{cm}$ tall is placed $25\,\text{cm}$ in front of a convex mirror of focal length $20\,\text{cm}$. Find the image distance.
examples.solution:
1. Sign convention: $u = -25\,\text{cm}$, $f = +20\,\text{cm}$ (convex).
  2. $\frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{f} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{20} - \frac{1}{-25} = \frac{1}{20} + \frac{1}{25}$.
  3. $\frac{1}{v} = \frac{5 + 4}{100} = \frac{9}{100}$.
  4. $v = \frac{100}{9} \approx +11.1\,\text{cm}$.

Answer: $v \approx +11.1\,\text{cm}$ — the image is virtual, behind the mirror.

examples.problem: For the convex mirror in Example 3 ($u = -25\,\text{cm}$, $v = +11.1\,\text{cm}$, $h = 5\,\text{cm}$), find the magnification and the height of the image.
examples.solution:
1. $m = -\frac{v}{u} = -\frac{11.1}{-25} = +0.44$.
  2. The magnification is positive, so the image is virtual and erect; $|m| < 1$, so it is diminished.
  3. Image height $h' = m \times h = 0.44 \times 5 = 2.2\,\text{cm}$.

Answer: $m = +0.44$; the image is virtual, erect and $2.2\,\text{cm}$ tall.

examples.problem: An object is placed $10\,\text{cm}$ in front of a concave mirror of focal length $15\,\text{cm}$. Find the image distance and nature.
examples.solution:
1. Sign convention: $u = -10\,\text{cm}$, $f = -15\,\text{cm}$.
  2. $\frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{f} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{-15} - \frac{1}{-10} = -\frac{1}{15} + \frac{1}{10}$.
  3. $\frac{1}{v} = \frac{-2 + 3}{30} = \frac{1}{30}$, so $v = +30\,\text{cm}$.
  4. $v$ is positive (behind the mirror), so the image is virtual.

Answer: $v = +30\,\text{cm}$ — the image is virtual and erect (object lies between P and F).

examples.problem: A concave mirror produces a real image magnified two times of an object placed $30\,\text{cm}$ in front of it. Find the focal length.
examples.solution:
1. Real, inverted image means $m = -2$. Given $u = -30\,\text{cm}$.
  2. $m = -\frac{v}{u}$, so $-2 = -\frac{v}{-30}$, giving $v = -60\,\text{cm}$.
  3. $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{-60} + \frac{1}{-30} = -\frac{1}{60} - \frac{2}{60} = -\frac{3}{60} = -\frac{1}{20}$.
  4. $f = -20\,\text{cm}$.

Answer: Focal length $= -20\,\text{cm}$ (concave mirror).

recap: New Cartesian sign convention: pole is the origin; distances along the incident light are positive, against it negative; heights up are positive, down negative.
Object distance $u$ is always negative; concave mirror $f$ is negative, convex mirror $f$ is positive.
Negative $m$ → real and inverted image; positive $m$ → virtual and erect image.

quiz.q: In the New Cartesian sign convention, the object distance for a mirror is always:
quiz.explanation: The object is placed in front of the mirror, against the incident light, so $u$ is always negative.

quiz.q: A magnification of $-2$ means the image is:
quiz.explanation: Negative $m$ means real and inverted; $|m| = 2 > 1$ means enlarged.

quiz.q: An object is $20\,\text{cm}$ from a concave mirror of focal length $10\,\text{cm}$ ($u=-20$, $f=-10$). The image distance $v$ is:
quiz.explanation: $\frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{-10} - \frac{1}{-20} = -\frac{1}{20}$, so $v = -20\,\text{cm}$ (object at C gives image at C).

topics.title: Refraction & Lenses
topics.concept:
When light passes from one transparent medium into another it changes speed, and as a result it bends. This bending of light at the boundary of two media is called refraction. Light bends because its speed is different in different media. Going from a rarer medium (such as air) into a denser one (such as glass or water), light slows down and bends towards the normal; going from denser to rarer it speeds up and bends away from the normal. A ray striking the surface along the normal (at $0^\circ$) passes straight through without bending.

Refraction obeys two laws. The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane. The second law is Snell's law: for a given pair of media, the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is constant, $\frac{\sin i}{\sin r} = n$, where $n$ is the refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first. The refractive index can also be written in terms of speeds:

  • $n = \frac{c}{v}$, where $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum (about $3 \times 10^8\,\text{m/s}$) and $v$ is the speed of light in the medium.

A lens is a piece of transparent material bounded by two curved surfaces. A convex (converging) lens is thicker in the middle and brings parallel rays to a real focus; a concave (diverging) lens is thinner in the middle and spreads parallel rays so they appear to come from a focus. Each lens has two foci, one on each side, and an optical centre O through which a ray passes undeviated.

The ray rules for lenses are straightforward. A ray parallel to the principal axis passes through the focus (convex) or appears to diverge from the focus (concave) after refraction; a ray through the optical centre goes straight on. Distances follow the same New Cartesian convention as for mirrors. The lens formula is $\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$ — note the minus sign, unlike the mirror formula. Magnification for a lens is $m = \frac{h'}{h} = \frac{v}{u}$. A convex lens has a positive focal length and a concave lens a negative one. The power of a lens measures how strongly it converges or diverges light: $P = \frac{1}{f}$, where $f$ is in metres and the unit of power is the dioptre (D). A convex lens has positive power and a concave lens has negative power.

examples.problem: The speed of light in glass is $2 \times 10^8\,\text{m/s}$ and in vacuum it is $3 \times 10^8\,\text{m/s}$. Find the refractive index of glass.
examples.solution:
1. Refractive index $n = \frac{c}{v}$.
  2. $n = \frac{3 \times 10^8}{2 \times 10^8}$.
  3. $n = 1.5$.

Answer: Refractive index of glass $= 1.5$.

examples.problem: The refractive index of water is $1.33$. Find the speed of light in water. (Take $c = 3 \times 10^8\,\text{m/s}$.)
examples.solution:
1. From $n = \frac{c}{v}$, we get $v = \frac{c}{n}$.
  2. $v = \frac{3 \times 10^8}{1.33}$.
  3. $v \approx 2.26 \times 10^8\,\text{m/s}$.

Answer: Speed of light in water $\approx 2.26 \times 10^8\,\text{m/s}$.

examples.problem: An object is placed $30\,\text{cm}$ in front of a convex lens of focal length $20\,\text{cm}$. Find the position of the image.
examples.solution:
1. Sign convention: $u = -30\,\text{cm}$, $f = +20\,\text{cm}$ (convex).
  2. Lens formula: $\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$, so $\frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{f} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{20} + \frac{1}{-30}$.
  3. $\frac{1}{v} = \frac{3 - 2}{60} = \frac{1}{60}$.
  4. $v = +60\,\text{cm}$.

Answer: $v = +60\,\text{cm}$ — a real, inverted image is formed $60\,\text{cm}$ on the other side of the lens.

examples.problem: For the lens in Example 3 ($u = -30\,\text{cm}$, $v = +60\,\text{cm}$), find the magnification and describe the image.
examples.solution:
1. For a lens, $m = \frac{v}{u} = \frac{60}{-30}$.
  2. $m = -2$.
  3. Negative $m$ means real and inverted; $|m| = 2 > 1$ means enlarged twice.

Answer: $m = -2$; the image is real, inverted and twice the size of the object.

examples.problem: Find the power of a convex lens of focal length $25\,\text{cm}$.
examples.solution:
1. First convert focal length to metres: $f = 25\,\text{cm} = 0.25\,\text{m}$.
  2. Power $P = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{0.25}$.
  3. $P = +4\,\text{D}$ (positive, as it is a convex lens).

Answer: Power $= +4\,\text{D}$.

examples.problem: A concave lens has a focal length of $50\,\text{cm}$. Calculate its power.
examples.solution:
1. A concave lens has a negative focal length: $f = -50\,\text{cm} = -0.5\,\text{m}$.
  2. $P = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{-0.5}$.
  3. $P = -2\,\text{D}$.

Answer: Power $= -2\,\text{D}$.

recap: Refraction is the bending of light at the boundary of two media due to a change in speed.
Snell's law: $\frac{\sin i}{\sin r} = n$; refractive index $n = \frac{c}{v}$.
Convex lens converges light (positive $f$, positive power); concave lens diverges light (negative $f$, negative power).
Power of a lens: $P = \frac{1}{f}$ (with $f$ in metres), measured in dioptre (D).

quiz.q: Light going from air into glass bends:
quiz.explanation: Glass is denser than air, so light slows down and bends towards the normal.

quiz.q: The refractive index of a medium is given by:
quiz.explanation: Refractive index $n = \frac{c}{v}$, the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to that in the medium.
For lenses the formula is $\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$ (note the minus sign).

options: greater than the angle of reflection
equal to the angle of reflection
less than the angle of reflection
questions.explanation: The first law of reflection states $\angle i = \angle r$.

questions.q: The focal length of a spherical mirror is related to its radius of curvature by:
questions.explanation: For a spherical mirror, $f = \frac{R}{2}$.

questions.q: Which mirror is used as a reflector in vehicle headlights?
questions.explanation: A concave mirror with the bulb at its focus produces a strong parallel beam.

questions.q: The centre of the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror is called the:
questions.explanation: The geometric centre of the mirror's surface is the pole (P).

questions.q: A convex mirror always forms an image that is:
questions.explanation: A convex mirror gives a virtual, erect, diminished image for every object position.

questions.q: In the New Cartesian sign convention, the focal length of a concave mirror is taken as:
questions.explanation: A concave mirror has a negative focal length in the New Cartesian convention.

questions.q: The mirror formula is:
questions.explanation: For mirrors, $\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$.

questions.q: Magnification produced by a mirror is given by:
questions.explanation: For mirrors, $m = -\frac{v}{u} = \frac{h'}{h}$.

questions.q: A concave mirror forms a real, inverted image of the same size as the object. The object is at the:
questions.explanation: When the object is at C, the image is at C — real, inverted and the same size.

questions.q: Bending of light as it passes from one transparent medium to another is called:

questions.explanation: Light slows down in the denser medium and bends towards the normal.

questions.q: The lens formula is:
questions.explanation: For lenses, $\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$.

questions.q: The SI unit of the power of a lens is the:
questions.explanation: Power of a lens, $P = \frac{1}{f}$ (in metres), is measured in dioptre (D).

questions.q: A convex lens of focal length $50\,\text{cm}$ has a power of:
An object is placed $30\,\text{cm}$ from a convex lens of focal length $15\,\text{cm}$ ($u=-30$, $f=+15$). The image distance is:
questions.explanation: $\frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{15} + \frac{1}{-30} = \frac{1}{30}$, so $v = +30\,\text{cm}$ (object at 2F).

questions.q: The speed of light in a medium of refractive index $1.5$ is (taking $c = 3 \times 10^8\,\text{m/s}$):
questions.explanation: $v = \frac{c}{n} = \frac{3 \times 10^8}{1.5} = 2 \times 10^8\,\text{m/s}$.

questions.q: For a lens, the magnification is given by:
questions.explanation: For lenses, $m = \frac{v}{u} = \frac{h'}{h}$ (no minus sign, unlike mirrors).

imo.title: Light – Reflection and Refraction — Olympiad Test

questions.q: A concave mirror of focal length $12\,\text{cm}$ forms a real image twice the size of the object. The object distance is:
questions.explanation: Real image, $m=-2 \Rightarrow v=2u$. Then $\frac{1}{v}+\frac{1}{u}=\frac{1}{2u}+\frac{2}{2u}=\frac{3}{2u}=\frac{1}{-12}$, giving $2u=-36$, so $u=-18\,\text{cm}$ (and $v=-36\,\text{cm}$).

questions.q: Light of speed $3 \times 10^8\,\text{m/s}$ in vacuum travels through a medium at $1.2 \times 10^8\,\text{m/s}$. The refractive index of the medium is:
Two thin lenses of powers $+3\,\text{D}$ and $-1\,\text{D}$ are kept in contact. The power of the combination is:
questions.explanation: Powers in contact add: $P = 3 + (-1) = +2\,\text{D}$.

questions.q: An object is at the focus of a concave mirror. The image is formed at:
questions.explanation: Rays from an object at F become parallel after reflection, so the image is at infinity.

questions.q: A convex lens forms a virtual, erect and enlarged image. The object must be placed:
options: between F and the optical centre
questions.explanation: Only when the object is between F and O does a convex lens form a virtual, erect, magnified image (magnifying-glass action).

questions.q: A concave mirror has $f = -10\,\text{cm}$. An object placed at $u=-10\,\text{cm}$ produces an image:
questions.explanation: Object at F: $\frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{f} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{-10} - \frac{1}{-10} = 0$, so $v \to \infty$.

questions.q: A lens has a power of $-2.5\,\text{D}$. Its focal length and type are:
questions.explanation: $f = \frac{1}{P} = \frac{1}{-2.5} = -0.4\,\text{m} = -40\,\text{cm}$; negative power means a concave lens.

questions.q: A ray of light travels from glass ($n=1.5$) into air. Compared with glass, in air the light:
options: slows down and bends towards the normal
speeds up and bends away from the normal
speeds up and bends towards the normal
questions.explanation: Air is rarer, so light speeds up and bends away from the normal.

questions.q: An object 2 cm tall is placed 10 cm from a convex lens of focal length 20 cm. The image is:
questions.explanation: $\frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{20} + \frac{1}{-10} = -\frac{1}{20}$, so $v=-20$; $m = \frac{v}{u} = \frac{-20}{-10} = +2$, image $= 2 \times 2 = 4\,\text{cm}$, virtual and erect.

questions.q: A plane mirror is rotated by $10^\circ$ while the incident ray is fixed. The reflected ray turns by:
questions.explanation: When a plane mirror turns by an angle $\theta$ with a fixed incident ray, the reflected ray turns by $2\theta = 20^\circ$.

questions.q: A convex mirror of focal length $15\,\text{cm}$ has an object at $u=-30\,\text{cm}$. The magnification is:
For the same object distance, which combination gives a real, magnified image?
options: concave mirror with object between F and C
questions.explanation: A concave mirror with the object between F and C forms a real, inverted, magnified image; convex mirrors and concave lenses give only virtual diminished images.

questions.q: A convex lens of focal length 10 cm and a concave lens of focal length 10 cm are placed in contact. The combination behaves as:
options: a convex lens of f = 5 cm
a concave lens of f = 5 cm
a plane glass plate (no converging or diverging)
a convex lens of f = 20 cm
questions.explanation: $P = \frac{1}{0.1} + \frac{1}{-0.1} = 0$, so the combination has zero power and acts like a plane plate.
